opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is this: the world has spent the last few years obsessing over training, but the real cost and the real bottleneck of AI is moving to inference. Every time someone chats with a model, runs an agent, or generates code, that's inference. And as models get used more and more, especially with reasoning and agentic workloads that produce huge numbers of tokens, serving efficiency becomes the thing that decides whether an AI product is economically viable at all.

That's where we come from. Our team built SGLang as an open-source project, starting from research at Berkeley and Stanford, and it has grown into one of the most widely used inference engines. It's running in production at large companies and cloud providers, on a huge range of hardware. So we're not starting from a slide deck. We're starting from a system that people already depend on, and from a community that keeps pushing it forward.

Second, the team. Building a high-performance inference stack is very hard. You need people who understand systems, compilers, GPU kernels, distributed scheduling, and the models themselves, all at once. We've been doing exactly that for years, and a lot of the ideas that are now standard in the field, like efficient KV cache reuse and structured generation, came out of this line of work.

Third, timing. The model landscape keeps changing: new architectures, mixture-of-experts, long context, multimodal, new chips from different vendors. Every change breaks something in the serving layer. Companies don't want to rebuild their infrastructure every six months. They want a partner who stays at the frontier and makes it just work, with the best performance per dollar. That's the value we provide.

So for an investor, the logic is: inference is becoming one of the largest compute markets in the world, efficiency there translates directly into money saved, and we already have the technology, the adoption, and the people to lead that layer. Open source gives us the distribution and trust; the company lets us turn that into products and services that enterprises are willing to pay for.

r001.rationale: The response cites high performance and serving efficiency, but gives no demonstrated speed result as evidence of future potential.

r002.rationale: It ties investment value to helping companies serve AI workloads efficiently, make AI products economically viable, and turn AI infrastructure into products and services customers will pay for.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd put it in three parts.

First, the problem is real and it's growing. Everyone has spent the last few years talking about training, but the cost that actually scales with usage is inference. Every time someone calls a model, that's a GPU doing work, and as models get used in agents, in long-running workflows, in products with millions of users, inference becomes the dominant cost line. Even a few percentage points of efficiency gain on that is enormous in absolute terms, and we're not talking about a few percentage points. Serving systems today are still far from what the hardware can theoretically deliver.

Second, we didn't start with a business plan and then look for a technology. We started with SGLang, which is an open-source serving engine that came out of research, and it earned adoption on its own merits. People run it because it's fast, because it handles things like structured output and prefix caching and multi-model workloads well, and because the community around it moves quickly. That gives us something most startups don't have on day one: real users at serious scale, running real production traffic, telling us exactly where the pain is. The company exists to take that foundation and make it dependable, supportable, and easy to adopt for teams that don't want to run infrastructure themselves.

Third, the team. The people building this are the ones who built the core system and who've been working on the hard systems problems in LLM serving for years. In infrastructure, that matters a lot. The gap between a good serving engine and a great one is in the details, the scheduling, the memory management, the kernels, how you handle disaggregated prefill and decode across a cluster. That's not something you can hire for quickly.

And I'd say one more thing, which is about timing. The model layer is becoming more open and more competitive, and when that happens, the value shifts to whoever can run those models best. We want to be the layer that every model, open or proprietary, runs on top of. If you believe inference demand keeps growing, and I don't see how it doesn't, then being the most efficient and most trusted way to serve that demand is a very good place to be.

r001.rationale: The response cites SGLang’s speed and adoption at serious scale, then connects its serving foundation to the company’s potential to deliver efficient inference as demand grows.

r002.rationale: It describes making AI serving dependable and easy for teams that do not want to run the infrastructure themselves, enabling them to use models in agents, workflows, and products.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame it around three questions: Are we solving a problem that really matters? Can we turn that solution into a sustainable business? And why is our team positioned to execute?

For me, the investment case has to connect those three things. An exciting technology is a starting point, but customers need a clear reason to choose the product and keep using it. And as the company grows, we need to show that the economics work and that our advantage can strengthen.

That’s how I’d want investors to assess us: the evidence behind the opportunity, the assumptions we still need to test, and what their capital would help us prove next.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the investment case and what the company must prove, but does not present demonstrated speed as evidence of future potential.

r002.rationale: The response mentions technology and customers generally, but does not ground investment value in enabling other companies to create value through AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d frame it around three questions: Are we solving a problem customers urgently need solved? Can we turn that demand into a sustainable business? And why is our team positioned to win?

For me, the investment case has to connect those three things. A large market alone isn’t enough—you need evidence that customers value what you’re building and a clear reason your advantage can grow over time. That’s the case I’d want to demonstrate, rather than simply asking investors to believe in a vision.

r001.rationale: It asks for evidence of customer value and a growing advantage, but does not mention the company’s demonstrated speed or present speed as evidence of future potential.

r002.rationale: It discusses customer demand, a sustainable business, and team advantage without grounding investment value in enabling other companies to create value through AI.
